topic: making heather mead: a stuck must, staged nutrient, racking off the lees and ageing before bottling

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-6)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: refraktometr (areometr zajety w en-16)

base: I have set my first mead going and the must has stopped bubbling after only nine days.
An oak cask stands in the cellar and held a batch of cider for two winters.
A refractometer sits on the shelf and I take a reading from every jar I fill.
I mixed three pounds of heather honey to the gallon and pitched a wine yeast on top.
Has the ferment stuck already, or does mead simply finish faster than I had expected?
It has stuck, since nine days is far too short for that weight of honey to be worked through.
Honey carries almost no nitrogen, so the yeast starves long before the sugar is gone.
Add nutrient in three small doses over the first week rather than all at the start.
Rouse the jar daily as well, because yeast that settles early tends to stop working for good.
I added nutrient in stages to the second batch and roused the jar every morning.
That one ran for five weeks and the refractometer shows it far drier than the first.
The jar has thrown a thick bed of lees and the liquid above it is still cloudy.
When should I rack it off, and does the cloudiness clear on its own in time?
Rack as soon as the lees are a finger deep, which is usually three weeks after the ferment ends.
Lees left too long give a bready taste that no amount of ageing will take away again.
Cloudiness falls out slowly in the cold, so put the jar somewhere unheated after racking.
Rack a second time two months later and you will rarely need to fine it at all.
I racked at three weeks and again in the new year and the mead has fallen bright.
The oak cask is standing empty and I have wondered about ageing this batch in it.
It is a five gallon cask and my batch runs to a little under four.
I could top it up with water, or I could keep the mead in glass instead.
Which would you do, given that the cask has held nothing but cider so far?
Keep it in glass, because a part filled cask gives you far more air than mead can stand.
Air is what turns a good mead thin and sharp, and it happens in weeks rather than months.
If you want oak, hang a few toasted staves in the jar and taste every fortnight.
Cider in the wood will also have left tannin that overwhelms a light heather mead.
Fill the cask properly one day with a larger batch, and it will serve you very well.
I hung two toasted staves in the jar and pulled them out again after five weeks.
The mead has a little oak about it now without losing the heather at all.
I would like to bottle it, though I am nervous about a ferment starting again.
How long should it stand quiet before bottling is safe, and at what temperature?
Give it three months with no movement at all, kept somewhere between ten and fifteen degrees.
Warm it for a fortnight before bottling, since a hidden yeast will show itself when roused.
If nothing stirs at all in that fortnight, the mead is as safe as it will ever be.
Bottle into thick glass regardless, because a heather mead can surprise you a year later.
I warmed it for a fortnight and nothing stirred, so I bottled into champagne glass.
The first bottle was opened at midsummer and tasted thin and rather sharp to me.
The rest are lying in the cellar and I am wondering whether to leave them alone.
Does a young mead of this kind come round, or is that thinness there for good?
It comes round, and a heather mead at six months is no guide whatever to its later self.
Thinness at that age is mostly the acid standing forward before the honey comes back.
Leave the bottles two years on their sides in the cellar and open one each autumn.
The change between the second and the third autumn is usually the one that surprises people.
